extracted.intended_audience: prospective reporters, newsroom staff, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on both newspaper production (mechanical/printing/business) and news-story writing: recognizing news values, sources, and practical methods for gathering and presenting news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading / Galley-proof corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection of typographical errors. A corrected galley proof will be returned in the form shown in the specimen proof sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make corrections on the galley proof to catch typographical errors before the form is locked for stereotyping; use specimen proof sheets as reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Form (page composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: After all corrections have been made and the position of the story in the paper has been determined by the news editor, it is inserted in its proper place among other articles which together make up a page of type, or what printers know as a form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positioning is determined by the news editor; the form is locked in a chase and moved to stereotyping; correct placement affects how pages are assembled for printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyping process
rubrics_metrics.description: The form is placed face up, tissue paper and damp blanket laid over the type, pressure applied by a revolving steel drum, then intense heat bakes the moist paper into a stiff flat matrix of the type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple layers of tissue, moisture, pressure, and rapid heat to create a durable paper matrix for casting plates; this produces the matrix for the autoplate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autoplate / casting plates
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper matrix is bent to the shape of the impressing cylinder and put into an autoplate, which presses molten metal upon the paper matrix, cools the metal, and produces cylindrical plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autoplate produces duplicates rapidly (every 15–20 seconds) so several impressions of the same page may be made at once; appropriate for larger papers needing many impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-room machinery adaptability and capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Presses are highly complicated and adaptable to running full, half, or third capacity; large presses fold, cut, paste, and count, producing tens of thousands of papers per hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose press size and configuration according to required output; understand limits (e.g., double-sextuple press limit of 144,000 twelve-page papers an hour) for planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitting plates on press cylinders / last-minute pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotyped plates for inside pages are screwed on cylinders half an hour or more before press time; pages with the latest news are held until the last possible moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold late news and title page items to the end; clamp locking levers only when final; timing determines whether late copy can be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-to-end printing workflow timing
rubrics_metrics.description: As cylinders revolve, inked rollers transfer type to the paper, which is drawn from large rolls, cut into pages, folded, and counted, with the whole time from last story chute to delivery to newsboys often not exceeding ten minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate city room output and press-room operations to minimize latency between copy completion and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed devices for late news (the 'fudge')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'fudge' is a small printing cylinder with a diminutive curved chase holding a few linotype slugs, keyed to a blank left in a stereotyped front page so the emergency cylinder prints last-minute copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the fudge to print directly from linotype slugs and avoid stereotyping time; key it to the blank on a pre-stereotyped page for seamless appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special composing machines and dedicated telegraph lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Great newspapers place a composing machine near the fudge with a special telegraph wire and operator to read news direct from the wire to the compositor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dedicated equipment and staffing to route late-wire copy quickly to the press-room composing area for immediate printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance headlines and held plates for predicted outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When an outcome can be predicted, advance headlines are set up and held ready to be clamped on the press (examples: two heads held awaiting a knockout).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare probable headlines in advance and keep them locked on the press to enable immediate publication when the event occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-department organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The business department is divided into divisions (circulation manager, advertising manager, cashier) supervised by the business manager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize responsibilities clearly across circulation, advertising, and cashier functions under overall business management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation manager duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution of large numbers of papers, supervision of canvassers for subscriptions, organization of newsboys, and advertising of the paper's features to attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage logistics (trains, wagons, newsboys), promote goodwill activities (e.g., free classified lists) when appropriate to boost circulation, and advertise forthcoming features to gain buyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising manager duties and ad placement strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent on circulation for rates; directs advertising solicitors; advises on place, price, space, and character of advertisements; accepts or rejects ads (e.g., liquor, questionable ads may be barred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place ads where they fit readership (back page > inside > next to reading matter > columns); selectively accept ads for financial gain while maintaining standards; use exchanges and audited statements to attract advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cashier / counting-room responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Directs payroll and all receipts and disbursements of the paper; keeps the books of the publishing company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain accurate financial records and handle payments to staff and suppliers; knowledge of bookkeeping and banking is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of news writing (four requisites)
rubrics_metrics.description: To write successful news stories, four requisites are necessary: the power to estimate news values properly, the stories to write, the ability to work rapidly, and the power to present facts accurately and interestingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop news judgment, cultivate story leads, work quickly under deadline, and craft copy that is both accurate and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nose for news (recognition of news values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of news values is put first because without a 'nose for news' — the ability to recognize a story when one sees it — a reporter cannot hope to succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train intuition to spot stories; study examples of good and bad leads to learn what constitutes news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of news
rubrics_metrics.description: News may be defined as any accurate fact or idea that will interest a large number of readers; of two stories, the accurate one that interests the greater number is the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accuracy and audience interest; unusualness, timeliness, and enormity add interest but are not essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (Accuracy First)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy First is the slogan of the modern newspaper. If a piece of news is untrue, it is worthless and undermines public confidence; rumors may be published only as unverified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts before publication; when publishing unverified reports, label them as rumors to avoid misleading readers and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest / provoking thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Any item of news that presents a new problem or situation that will provoke thought in the minds of a considerable number of readers is interesting; the most interesting story presents a new problem to the greatest number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories to highlight the new problem or situation; aim to engage readers' thinking without overcomplicating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness is of vital worth; words like to-day, this morning, this afternoon should appear if possible in every story; freshness is nearly a requisite in daily newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angle stories to emphasize current relevance; use temporal markers to convey immediacy when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closeness (nearness in place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other things being equal, the worth of a story varies in inverse proportion to its closeness in time and place; reporters should localize stories and draw them close to readers' everyday lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localize national or distant events when possible by connecting them to local people, places, or reactions to increase reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for extremes / record-breaking features
rubrics_metrics.description: The public loves extremes; a record breaker in anything (largest, foulest, boldest, fastest) is new problem and will be read with eager joy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for superlative or record-setting angles to make ordinary events newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: The unusual / abnormal
rubrics_metrics.description: The exceptional, the unusual, the abnormal (e.g., a calf with two heads, a dog committing suicide) are of exceptional interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight unique or quirky elements of a story to attract reader attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contests and struggles
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of contests (athletic, business, political, etc.) inject the element of struggle for supremacy and are always interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize conflict and competition in coverage to provide an elemental, thrilling appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helplessness / human-interest 'sob stories'
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories depicting the joys or sufferings of the very old or very young or those unable to struggle tend to compel sympathy and have emotional appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compassionate, factual storytelling to illustrate helplessness and possibly prompt practical help; avoid exploitative sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominent persons attract interest
rubrics_metrics.description: News about prominent men and women, however trivial, is always of interest and varies with the prominence of the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story involves a person with high social or professional position, give it prominence even if details are minor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-known places increase value
rubrics_metrics.description: Items about noted or notorious places carry added interest by virtue of their previous note or notoriety (e.g., Reno vs. Rome, Georgia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set stories in well-known locations when possible to leverage existing reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and financial interest relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that bear directly on the personal or financial interests of readers (prices, taxes, styles, shortages) will be cordially received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor markets, local business, and consumer trends; include practical information (prices, shortages, style changes) that affects readers' everyday lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary requirement for story material
rubrics_metrics.description: The only requirements of an event or idea to make it good story material are that it be presented accurately and possess interest for a goodly number of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accuracy and audience interest as primary filters when deciding what to cover and how to angle it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gathering news with a definite plan
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter never leaves the city room without a definite idea of where he is going; reporters do not wander aimlessly hoping for accidents to happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan beats and visits; have specific objectives and sources to cover rather than relying on chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police blotter / slips as primary news source
rubrics_metrics.description: Police reports (slips) record fires, robberies, murders, accidents, and mishaps; these brief bulletins are typical advance notices for reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use police slips for prompt, accurate accounts of local crimes and accidents; understand notation (officer signed, precinct, time) to follow up effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest sheets for public-record information
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrest sheets record all arrests and are open to public inspection; from these a reporter can get brief but prompt and accurate accounts of accidents and crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult arrest sheets for verification and leads; use entries to track pending cases and follow up on disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other official records as news sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors report births/deaths/contagious diseases; coroners report suspicious deaths; county clerks record marriage licenses; recorders of deeds register property transfers; building inspectors record condemned buildings and permits; hotels list important guests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop routine visitation of these offices and sources to harvest regular, verifiable news items relevant to the neighborhood.
